169.title: Al-Fil: the elephant
169.hook: the army of the elephant and the birds with stones (Surah 105)
169.howItsDone: Surah al-Fil is recited in the prayers, and the story of Abraha and the Year of the Elephant is taught as part of the Prophet's biography, since tradition places his birth in that year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Quraysh, the tribe that was fed and kept safe. Your line was fed and safe. Before you ate, did you notice both? Day one hundred sixty-nine.

A desert town with no walls and no army. Coming up the road from the south is a real army, and with it an elephant, maybe more than one, marching toward the one building the town is known for. The townspeople do the only thing they can. They leave, and they go up into the hills to watch. This happened, according to Muslim tradition, in the year the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was born. Today: Al-Fil, the elephant.
screen: `A TOWN WITH NO WALLS.` → `AN ARMY WITH AN ELEPHANT.` → `THEY WATCH FROM THE HILLS.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred five opens, in Pickthall's translation: Hast thou not seen how thy Lord dealt with the owners of the Elephant? The Qur'an tells it in five lines and doesn't name anyone. The historians and commentators fill in the names. The army came from Yemen, led by a ruler named Abraha, who, the story goes, had built a great church and wanted the Arabs to make pilgrimage there instead of to the Ka'bah. So he marched to destroy it. There's a famous scene in the early biography of the Prophet. Abraha's men seized camels belonging to Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's grandfather and a leader of Mecca. He went to Abraha and asked for his camels back. Abraha was surprised: I've come to destroy your holy House, and you ask about camels? And Abd al-Muttalib is remembered as saying: I am the lord of the camels. The House has its own Lord, who will protect it. Then the surah tells what happened. The plan came to nothing. Allah sent birds in flocks, ababil, pelting the army with stones of baked clay, and left them like chewed-up straw. Tradition says the Arabs counted years from it: the Year of the Elephant. Tradition places the Prophet's birth in that year, around five hundred seventy. So the surah reminds Quraysh of something their own elders saw. They didn't defend the House. They couldn't. They went up into the hills. The house was defended.
screen: `THE OWNERS OF THE ELEPHANT.` · `I AM THE LORD OF THE CAMELS.` · `BIRDS IN FLOCKS, STONES OF CLAY.` · `THE YEAR OF THE ELEPHANT.` · then, large: `THE HOUSE WAS DEFENDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and remember a time you were protected, when something could have gone badly and didn't. A near miss on the road. A diagnosis that came back clear. Someone who stepped in for you. Notice how little of it you controlled. Stay with the memory for a while, and let yourself feel the relief again. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for it, as if it happened today. The bell holds the time.
Al-Fil. The elephant, the name of Surah one hundred five, about the army that marched on the Ka'bah. Today's word.

Your line: the house was defended. When you catch yourself trying to guard everything alone today, remember Abd al-Muttalib and his camels. Do your part, and notice what was never yours to guard. Day one hundred sixty-nine.

170.title: Al-Humazah: the slanderer
170.hook: woe to the backbiter who counts his money and thinks it will keep him (Surah 104)
170.howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Humazah in the prayers, and Islamic teaching treats backbiting (ghibah) and slander as serious wrongs; many try to leave a gathering or change the subject when others are mocked.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Fil, the army of the elephant, and a grandfather who asked for his camels. Your line was the house was defended. Did you do your part and leave the rest? Day one hundred seventy.

He turns up at work, at school, at family dinners. The one who does impressions of a coworker the moment she leaves the room. The eye-roll across the table. The group chat screenshot with a laughing emoji. It feels small, and it feels safe, especially when you're the one with more money, more status, more followers. Today's surah has a word for this person, and it doesn't treat it as small at all. Nine lines, and it opens with woe. Today: Al-Humazah, the slanderer.
screen: `THE IMPRESSION BEHIND HER BACK.` → `THE EYE-ROLL, THE SCREENSHOT.` → `IT OPENS WITH WOE.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred four begins, in Pickthall's translation: Woe unto every slandering traducer, Who hath gathered wealth of this world and arrangeth it. He thinketh that his wealth will render him immortal. In Arabic the first line is two sharp words: humazah, lumazah. Commentators give them related shades. One is mocking with gestures, the look, the smirk, the pointed finger. The other is wounding with the tongue, especially behind someone's back. Both are forms of the same thing: making someone smaller so you can feel bigger. And then the surah does something revealing. It moves straight from mockery to money. The mocker is also the man counting his wealth, over and over, arranging it. The two go together. In the surah's picture, contempt for people and trust in money come from the same place: the belief that you're safe, above it all, untouchable. He thinks his wealth will make him last forever. The surah says no, and describes a fire that reaches the heart, the place where the contempt began. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave a plain definition of backbiting, recorded in Sahih Muslim. He asked his companions: do you know what backbiting is? It's mentioning your brother in a way he would dislike. Someone asked: what if it's true? He said: if it's true, that's backbiting. If it's false, that's slander. So the test isn't whether the joke is accurate. It's whether they'd be hurt to hear it. Money won't keep you. Neither will the laugh at someone else's expense.
screen: `HUMAZAH, LUMAZAH — THE LOOK, THE TONGUE.` · `FROM MOCKERY STRAIGHT TO MONEY.` · `HE THINKS HIS WEALTH WILL KEEP HIM.` · `EVEN IF IT'S TRUE, IT'S BACKBITING.` · then, large: `MONEY WON'T KEEP YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and think honestly about the last time you mocked someone, out loud, in a message, or just with a look. No need for guilt; just see it clearly. What were you protecting? Then picture that person hearing it. Let the picture be real for a moment. Now decide: for the rest of today, no mocking. Not in words, not in texts, not with your eyes. The bell holds the time.
Al-Humazah. The slanderer, the one who mocks and belittles; the name of Surah one hundred four. Today's word.
Your line: money won't keep you. Go one day without mocking anyone. When the joke at someone's expense rises up, let it pass unsaid. Day one hundred seventy.

171.title: Al-'Asr: by time
171.hook: by time, people are in loss, except those who believe, do good, and urge truth and patience (Surah 103)
171.howItsDone: Al-'Asr is among the most memorized surahs and is often recited in the prayers; its name is shared with the afternoon prayer, and many Muslims recall it when they think about how they spend their time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Humazah, the mocker who counts his money. Your line was money won't keep you. Did a joke at someone's expense rise up, and did you let it pass? Day one hundred seventy-one.

Open the screen-time report on your phone. Most people do it once, wince, and never do it again. Four hours a day. Twenty-eight hours a week. Numbers you'd never agree to if someone asked you to spend them up front. Time goes the way ice melts: not all at once, just steadily, while you're looking at something else. Today's surah is one of the shortest in the Qur'an, three lines, and it opens by swearing an oath by that very thing. Today: Al-'Asr, by time.
screen: `THE SCREEN-TIME REPORT.` → `TIME MELTS LIKE ICE.` → `AN OATH BY TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole surah in Pickthall's translation: By the declining day, Lo! man is in a state of loss, Save those who believe and do good works, and exhort one another to truth and exhort one another to endurance. The first word is al-'asr. It has several meanings, and scholars keep them all. It's the late afternoon, the declining day, when the light starts to go; it's the name of the afternoon prayer, 'asr. And it's time itself, the age, an era. The root carries a sense of pressing, of squeezing something out. The afternoon is the part of the day when you feel the day being squeezed. When the Qur'an swears by something, it's asking you to look at it closely. So look at time. Then the verdict: the human being is in loss. Not some people. All of us, by default. Time is running out, every hour, like capital being spent. That's the plain math of being mortal. And then the exception. Except, and the rest of the surah is the exception. Those who believe. Those who do good. Those who urge one another to truth. Those who urge one another to patience. Tomorrow we'll look at those four closely. Today, just the first half: the oath and the loss. The surah doesn't tell you to panic. It tells you to notice. Every hour is being spent on something. By time is a question: on what?
screen: `AL-'ASR — THE DECLINING DAY, AND TIME.` · `AN OATH SAYS: LOOK CLOSELY.` · `THE HUMAN IS IN LOSS.` · `EXCEPT: THE WAY OUT OF LOSS.` · then, large: `BY TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Look at the clock, and notice the time. Then choose, on purpose, how you'll spend the next five minutes after this lesson. Not scrolling by default. One thing, chosen: a call to your mother, a page of something good, a walk around the block, tidying one shelf. Right now, sit and let the seconds go by without filling them. Feel them pass. They're passing either way. The bell holds the time.
Al-'Asr. Time, the declining day, and the afternoon prayer; the name of Surah one hundred three. Today's word.
Your line: by time. Spend five minutes well on purpose today. When you notice the afternoon light starting to go, let it remind you. Day one hundred seventy-one.

172.title: Al-'Asr again: the four
172.hook: Imam al-Shafi'i said this surah alone would be enough guidance
172.howItsDone: Many Muslims know al-'Asr by heart and recite it in the prayers; teachers often use it as a summary of Islamic life, and some friends end a gathering by reciting it together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-'Asr, the oath by time and the verdict of loss. Your line was by time. Did you spend five minutes well, on purpose? What did you choose? Day one hundred seventy-two.

If you could keep only one page of advice for the rest of your life, what would be on it? People argue about this over dinner: one book, one verse, one sentence. Imam al-Shafi'i, the scholar of Islamic law whose name one of the Sunni schools still carries, had an answer about the Qur'an. He's reported to have said that if people reflected on this one surah, it would be enough for them. Three lines. Today: Al-'Asr again, the four.
screen: `ONE PAGE FOR THE REST OF YOUR LIFE.` → `IMAM AL-SHAFI'I.` → `IT WOULD BE ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: by time, the human being is in loss. Today, the exception, in Pickthall's words: Save those who believe and do good works, and exhort one another to truth and exhort one another to endurance. Four things. First, faith: iman, trust in Allah, the root under everything else. Second, good deeds: 'amal salih, faith that turns into hands. Here, as in other verses, the two come as a pair: belief, and the deeds that show it. Now the surprise. The last two are not things you do alone. The Arabic word is tawasaw: urge one another, counsel each other, a verb that only works between people. Urge one another to truth, al-haqq: what's right, what's real, even when it's awkward to say. And urge one another to patience, as-sabr: endurance, holding steady, not giving up on the right thing when it gets hard. So the way out of loss isn't a private self-improvement plan. It's a small community of people who keep each other honest and keep each other going. It's reported that when two companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ met, they wouldn't part until one of them had recited this surah to the other. That's what al-Shafi'i saw in it. Belief, action, and two kinds of friendship: the friend who tells you the truth, and the friend who helps you stay the course. Faith, good, truth, patience.
screen: `IMAN — FAITH.` · `'AMAL SALIH — GOOD DEEDS.` · `TAWASAW — URGE ONE ANOTHER.` · `TO TRUTH, AND TO PATIENCE.` · then, large: `FAITH, GOOD, TRUTH, PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the four in your life. Sit, and take them one at a time, a breath for each. Faith: where does your trust rest right now? Good: one thing you did this week that helped someone. Truth: who tells you the truth, even when it's hard to hear? Patience: who helps you keep going? Let a face come for each one. If a place is empty, just notice it. The bell holds the time.
Al-'Asr again. The four that keep a person from loss: faith, good deeds, urging one another to truth, and to patience. Today's word.
Your line: faith, good, truth, patience. Today, be one of the four for someone else. Tell a friend a kind truth, or help them hold on to something hard. Day one hundred seventy-two.

what it means: faith and good deeds, plus two things done together: urging one another to truth and to patience.

173.title: At-Takathur: more
173.hook: the race for more distracts you until the grave (Surah 102)
173.howItsDone: Muslims recite at-Takathur in the prayers and often quote it, with the hadith of 'my wealth, my wealth,' as a reminder against competing in possessions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-'Asr again, the four that keep a person from loss. Your line was faith, good, truth, patience. Were you one of the four for someone today? Day one hundred seventy-three.

The cart has three things in it. Then there's a banner: free shipping if you spend fifteen dollars more. So you add a fourth thing you didn't want five seconds ago. The feeling is familiar. More followers, a bigger house, a better phone, one more episode. Not because any of it is bad, but because more has its own pull, and it never says enough. Today's surah is eight lines about that pull, and its opening runs straight to the graveyard. Today: At-Takathur, more.
screen: `FIFTEEN DOLLARS MORE FOR FREE SHIPPING.` → `MORE NEVER SAYS ENOUGH.` → `STRAIGHT TO THE GRAVEYARD.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred two, in Pickthall's translation, begins: Rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you Until ye come to the graves. Takathur is from the root k-th-r, the same root as al-Kawthar a few days ago. Abundance was a gift. Takathur is a race: competing in having more, piling up to outdo each other. The difference is the direction. One looks at what you were given. The other looks sideways, at what the neighbor has. Commentators tell of two clans in Mecca who boasted about which had more men. When they ran out of the living, they went to the graveyard and counted the dead. Whether or not that story fits exactly, the surah's picture is sharp: the race for more keeps you busy right up until you visit the graves, and then you're in one. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ recited this surah and said, in a hadith in Sahih Muslim: the son of Adam says, my wealth, my wealth. But what do you really have of your wealth, except what you ate and used up, what you wore and wore out, or what you gave in charity and sent ahead? In another hadith, in Bukhari, he said that if a person had a valley full of gold, he'd want a second. The surah ends with a line about being asked, on that Day, about the pleasures you were given. Some commentators read it as a question of gratitude rather than a ban on enjoying them: did you notice them, or were you too busy chasing the next one? More is a distraction.
screen: `TAKATHUR — THE RACE FOR MORE.` · `COUNTING, ALL THE WAY TO THE GRAVES.` · `WHAT YOU ATE, WORE, AND GAVE.` · `ASKED ABOUT THE PLEASURES GIVEN.` · then, large: `MORE IS A DISTRACTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and think of one thing you've been meaning to buy. Picture it clearly. Now ask, honestly: do I need this, or do I want more? Either answer is fine. Then look around at what you already have, and pick one thing you've stopped noticing: a mug you love, a warm coat, a window. Look at it the way you looked at the thing you wanted. The bell holds the time.
At-Takathur. The race for more, piling up to outdo each other; the name of Surah one hundred two. Today's word.
Your line: more is a distraction. Don't buy one thing today that you were going to buy. Notice what the wanting feels like when you don't feed it. Day one hundred seventy-three.

174.title: Al-Qari'ah: the striking
174.hook: the Day people are like scattered moths and mountains like wool (Surah 101)
174.howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Qari'ah in the prayers; belief in the weighing of deeds on the Day of Judgment is part of Islamic creed, and good character is often taught as the heaviest deed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: At-Takathur, the race for more. Your line was more is a distraction. Did you skip one purchase, and what did the wanting feel like? Day one hundred seventy-four.

On a summer night, turn on the porch light and watch. Moths come from nowhere, dozens of them, flying in every direction, bumping into the glass, into each other, into you. No order, no plan. Just scattered. Then the mountains, solid rock for as long as anyone remembers, gone as loose as a handful of wool pulled apart. Those are the two pictures today's surah uses for a single moment, the Day everything is shaken loose. And then it asks one simple question. Today: Al-Qari'ah, the striking.
screen: `MOTHS AROUND THE PORCH LIGHT.` → `MOUNTAINS LIKE PULLED WOOL.` → `ONE SIMPLE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred one opens with a single word, repeated like a knock on the door. In Pickthall's translation: The Calamity! What is the Calamity? Ah, what will convey unto thee what the Calamity is! A day wherein mankind will be as thickly-scattered moths And the mountains will become as carded wool. Al-qari'ah comes from a root meaning to strike, to knock hard. It's one of the Qur'an's names for the Day of Judgment: the thing that strikes, the knock you can't ignore. Notice the surah's method. It asks: what is it? And then: what will tell you what it is? It admits the thing is beyond words, and gives you pictures instead. Then comes the question. The surah says that on that Day, whoever's scales are heavy will be in a life of contentment, and whoever's scales are light will have a pit for a home. That's it. Not how famous you were, not how much you had. Light or heavy. In Sunni creed the scales are real, weighing a person's deeds. And a hadith in Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud says what weighs most: nothing is heavier on the scale than good character. Not dramatic acts. Character: patience in traffic, honesty in a small deal, kindness to someone who can't repay it. The surah is short and loud, because it's meant to wake you. But what it wakes you to is quiet: the weight of ordinary deeds, adding up, every day.
screen: `AL-QARI'AH — THE KNOCK YOU CAN'T IGNORE.` · `SCATTERED MOTHS, CARDED WOOL.` · `THE SCALES: HEAVY OR LIGHT.` · `NOTHING HEAVIER THAN GOOD CHARACTER.` · then, large: `LIGHT OR HEAVY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: weigh one deed honestly. Sit, and pick one thing you did yesterday, just one. The way you spoke to someone, how you handled a task, a choice about money or time. Hold it in your mind like something in your hand. Does it feel heavy, full of care, or light, done carelessly? No judgment. Just an honest weighing. Then picture what would have made it heavier. The bell holds the time.
Al-Qari'ah. The striking, the knock: a name for the Day of Judgment, and the name of Surah one hundred one. Today's word.
Your line: light or heavy. Before one ordinary thing you do today, ask: will this be light, or heavy? Then give it a little more care. Day one hundred seventy-four.

175.title: Al-'Adiyat: the chargers
175.hook: by the panting horses, the human is ungrateful to his Lord (Surah 100)
175.howItsDone: Muslims recite al-'Adiyat in the prayers; its verse on human ingratitude is often quoted in teaching about shukr, gratitude shown in words and in action.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Qari'ah, the striking, and the scales. Your line was light or heavy. Did you give one ordinary thing a little more weight? Day one hundred seventy-five.

Hear it first. Hooves, pounding. Breath snorting out of a horse's nose in the cold. Sparks where hooves strike rock. A cloud of dust at dawn, and a line of riders charging straight into the middle of the enemy. Today's surah opens like the first thirty seconds of a war movie. Then it lands somewhere you wouldn't guess. After all that thunder, it points at something quiet, something inside every person. Today: Al-'Adiyat, the chargers.
screen: `HOOVES, BREATH, SPARKS, DUST.` → `A CHARGE AT DAWN.` → `THEN SOMETHING QUIET.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred opens with five oaths, all about the war horse. The ones that run panting. The ones that strike sparks. The ones that raid at dawn, raising dust, plunging into the crowd. Al-'adiyat means the runners, the chargers. Then the turn, in Pickthall's words: Lo! man is an ingrate unto his Lord. The word is kanud. The early scholar al-Hasan al-Basri explained it: the one who counts his misfortunes and forgets his blessings. Why horses? Commentators point to what a war horse is: an animal that gives everything for its rider. It runs until it pants, into danger, at dawn, because it was fed and cared for. Loyalty at full speed. And the human, fed and cared for far more, often doesn't even say thank you. The surah goes on: and he is a witness to that. Commentators differ on who the witness is; on one reading, it's the person himself. Deep down, he knows. And he is violent in his love of wealth. Then it reminds us of the day the graves are opened and what's in hearts is brought out. So what's the opposite of kanud? Shukr, gratitude, and gratitude here isn't a feeling you sit with. It moves, like the horses. It shows up in thank-yous said out loud, in giving back, in using a gift for what it was given for. And that ends a week of short, sharp surahs: the elephant, the mocker, time twice over, the race for more, the scales, and now the chargers. Gratitude charges forward.
